hints: Look very carefully at measurement 2. It is not an amount, it is a time. What does a low (short) time to make antibody after a booster tell you?
Remember the difference between circulating antibody in blood and memory cells waiting to respond. Which one gives fast secondary responses in active immunity, even ten years later?
walkthrough:
**Recall what vaccination gives**

Vaccination introduces antigen, so your own lymphocytes respond and make memory cells. That is active immunity, not passive immunity.

Active = you make your own memory cells. Passive = you are given ready-made antibodies.

**Interpret the three low values after ten years**

Measurement 1 is low: circulating antibody has fallen over ten years. That is normal, antibodies are broken down.

Measurement 3 is low: few virus-specific lymphocytes are found per cm3 of blood. Memory cells mainly live in lymph nodes, not circulating in large numbers.

Measurement 2 is low: the time taken to boost antibody is short. That means a very fast secondary response.

**Link fast response to memory cells**

Only memory B and memory T cells can give a rapid, large antibody rise on re-exposure. A short time in measurement 2 proves memory cells are still present.

So despite low antibody now, the person still has active immunity due to memory cells.

options.A: Correct. Vaccination gave active immunity and the fast booster response proves memory cells persist, even though circulating antibody is now low.
options.B: False. Low circulating antibody does not mean low immunity, because protection comes from memory cells that can rapidly make new antibody.
options.C: False. Memory cells must be present, because measurement 2 shows a fast (low time) secondary response after the booster.
options.D: False. Vaccination stimulates active immunity, not passive immunity, and passive immunity gives no memory cells and lasts only weeks.
